Determiners.question: Choose the appropriate quantifier: 'There is ______ hope of his recovery; the doctors have given up.'
Determiners.conceptTag: Little vs A Little vs Few
Determiners.explanation: 'Hope' is uncountable. 'Little' (without article) means 'hardly any / almost zero' (negative sense), whereas 'a little' means 'some, though not much' (positive sense).

Determiners.question: Fill in the blank: '______ knowledge is a dangerous thing.'
Determiners.explanation: 'A little knowledge' means 'a small amount of knowledge (some)', which can mislead a person into thinking they know everything.

Determiners.question: Choose the correct determiner: 'Do you have ______ complaints regarding the hostel facilities?'
Determiners.conceptTag: Some vs Any in Interrogatives and Negatives
Determiners.explanation: 'Any' is generally used in interrogative (question) and negative sentences, whereas 'some' is used in affirmative sentences and polite offers.

Determiners.question: Select the correct articles: 'He is ______ honest officer who graduated from ______ university in Delhi.'
Determiners.conceptTag: Phonetic Vowel vs Consonant Sound in Articles
Determiners.explanation: 'Honest' begins with a silent 'h' and a vowel sound (/ɒ/), taking 'an'. 'University' begins with a consonant glide sound (/juː/), taking 'a'.

Determiners.question: Differentiate between 'Each' and 'Every': 'There were two trees on ______ side of the narrow street.'
Determiners.conceptTag: Each (Two or more) vs Every (Three or more)
Determiners.explanation: 'Each' is used for two or more items (a street has only two sides), whereas 'every' is used only for sets of three or more.

Determiners.question: Choose the right quantifier: 'How ______ pages of this novel have you read so far?'
Determiners.explanation: 'Pages' is a plural countable noun, so it takes 'many'. 'Much' is used only with uncountable nouns.

Determiners.question: Fill in the blank: '______ the books you lent me last week were very informative.'
Determiners.explanation: 'Both' is used with plural countable nouns ('the books') and a plural verb ('were') when referring to two items together.

Determiners.question: Identify the correct determiner: '______ of the two candidates was found suitable for the post, so the interview panel rejected both.'
Determiners.conceptTag: Neither (of two) vs None (of three or more)
Determiners.explanation: When negating two items/persons, 'Neither' is used. 'None' is used for three or more.

Tenses.question: Choose the correct verb form: 'The patient ______ before the doctor arrived at the hospital.'
Tenses.conceptTag: Past Perfect for Earlier Past Action
Tenses.explanation: When two actions occur in the past, the earlier action takes the Past Perfect ('had died') and the later action takes the Simple Past ('arrived').

Tenses.question: Complete the sentence: 'Galileo proved that the Earth ______ around the Sun.'
Tenses.conceptTag: Universal Truth Exception in Past Sequence
Tenses.explanation: Even if the main clause verb ('proved') is in the past tense, a subordinate clause stating a universal scientific truth must remain in the Simple Present ('revolves').

Tenses.question: Identify the correct option: 'He walks as fast as he ______.'
Tenses.explanation: After 'as...as' or 'than', the tense aligns with the main clause. Since 'walks' is present, 'can' is required instead of past 'could'.

Tenses.question: Choose the correct sequence: 'She worked hard so that she ______ win the scholarship.'
Tenses.conceptTag: Purpose Clauses with 'So That' in Past
Tenses.explanation: When the principal clause is in the past tense ('worked'), a clause of purpose introduced by 'so that' or 'in order that' takes 'might' or 'could'.

Tenses.question: Fill in the blank: 'I ______ for my friend since 9 o'clock this morning, and he still hasn't arrived.'
Tenses.explanation: An action that began in the past ('since 9 o'clock') and is still continuing in the present requires the Present Perfect Continuous tense.

Tenses.question: Select the right verb: 'While I ______ the street, I saw an old school friend.'
Tenses.explanation: An ongoing background action in the past ('was crossing') interrupted by a shorter action ('saw') takes the Past Continuous tense.

Tenses.question: Complete the sentence: 'It is high time we ______ preparing for the final examinations.'
Tenses.conceptTag: Subjunctive Past after 'It is high time'
Tenses.explanation: The idiomatic expression 'It is time / It is high time + subject' is always followed by the Simple Past verb ('started') to indicate a present obligation.

Tenses.question: Choose the correct form: 'Five years have passed since I ______ my hometown.'
Tenses.explanation: When 'since' connects two clauses where the main clause is in the Present Perfect ('have passed'), the clause following 'since' takes the Simple Past ('left').

Modals.question: Which modal best expresses moral obligation or duty: 'We ______ respect our elderly parents and teachers.'
Modals.explanation: 'Ought to' specifically conveys moral duty, social obligation, or desirable ethical conduct.

Modals.question: Look at the clear blue sky; there isn't a single cloud. It ______ rain today, though anything is possible in the hills.
Modals.explanation: 'Might' expresses weak or remote possibility when current evidence makes the event unlikely.

Modals.question: What is the key difference between 'was able to' and 'could' when talking about a single past achievement?
options: 'Could' expresses general past ability, whereas 'was able to' is required for a specific successful action on one occasion
'Could' is used only for future events
'Was able to' cannot be used with living subjects
Both are strictly forbidden in formal grammar
Modals.correctAnswer: 'Could' expresses general past ability, whereas 'was able to' is required for a specific successful action on one occasion
Modals.conceptTag: General Past Ability vs Specific Achievement
Modals.explanation: For general past ability (e.g., 'I could swim when I was five'), 'could' works; for managing a specific one-time feat, 'was/were able to' is used.

Modals.question: Choose the correct modal for prohibition: 'Visitors ______ feed the wild animals in the zoological park; it is strictly illegal.'
Modals.conceptTag: Prohibition (Must not) vs Lack of Necessity (Need not)
Modals.explanation: 'Must not' indicates strict prohibition or rule violation, whereas 'need not' or 'don't have to' merely means something is optional.

Modals.question: Select the most formal modal for asking permission from an authority: '______ I come in, Sir?'
Modals.explanation: 'May' is the standard modal for polite, formal permission, whereas 'can' is informal and primarily denotes physical or mental ability.

Modals.question: Choose the right modal for absence of necessity: 'You ______ carry an umbrella; the weather forecast says it will be sunny all day.'
Modals.explanation: 'Needn't' (need not) indicates that an action is not necessary or required, without forbidding it.

Modals.question: Which modal gives strong advice in a medical context: 'You have a high fever; you ______ consult a physician immediately.'
Modals.explanation: 'Should' is used to offer strong advice, recommendations, or sensible courses of action.

Modals.question: Identify the correct deduction: 'The lights are on and his car is in the driveway; he ______ be at home.'
Modals.explanation: 'Must' is used to express strong logical deduction or certainty based on clear present evidence.

Subject–Verb Concord.question: Choose the correct verb: 'The quality of these mangoes ______ not very good.'
Subject–Verb Concord.conceptTag: Head Noun vs Prepositional Object Distractor
Subject–Verb Concord.explanation: The real subject is the singular head noun 'The quality', not the plural object of the preposition ('mangoes'). Hence singular 'is' is required.

Subject–Verb Concord.question: Complete the sentence: 'Neither the captain nor the players ______ arrived at the stadium yet.'
Subject–Verb Concord.explanation: With 'neither...nor' or 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Since 'players' is plural, the plural verb 'have' is used.

Subject–Verb Concord.question: Select the correct verb: 'The teacher, along with all her students, ______ visiting the science museum today.'
Subject–Verb Concord.conceptTag: Additive Phrases (Along with / As well as)
Subject–Verb Concord.explanation: When two nouns are joined by 'along with', 'as well as', 'together with', or 'besides', the verb agrees with the FIRST subject ('The teacher' -> 'is').

Subject–Verb Concord.question: Choose the right verb: 'Each of the participants ______ given a certificate of appreciation.'
Subject–Verb Concord.explanation: Pronouns like 'Each of', 'Every one of', 'Either of', and 'Neither of' are always grammatically singular and take a singular verb ('was').

Subject–Verb Concord.question: Identify the correct option: 'Mathematics ______ my favorite subject in school.'
Subject–Verb Concord.explanation: Nouns like 'Mathematics', 'Physics', 'Economics', 'News', and 'Measles' end in '-s' in form but are singular in meaning and take a singular verb.

Subject–Verb Concord.question: What is the grammatical difference between 'A number of students' and 'The number of students'?
options: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb; 'The number of' refers to a single numerical count and takes a singular verb
Both always take a singular verb
Both always take a plural verb
'A number of' takes a singular verb while 'The number of' takes a plural verb
Subject–Verb Concord.correctAnswer: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb; 'The number of' refers to a single numerical count and takes a singular verb
Subject–Verb Concord.explanation: 'A number of students ARE absent' (many students), whereas 'The number of students in this class IS forty' (the specific figure 40).

Subject–Verb Concord.question: Choose the correct verb: 'Fifty kilometers ______ a long distance to walk on foot.'
Subject–Verb Concord.conceptTag: Plural Units of Distance, Time, and Money
Subject–Verb Concord.explanation: When a plural noun denotes a specific quantity, distance, weight, or sum of money considered as a single whole, it takes a singular verb ('is').

Subject–Verb Concord.question: Select the correct verb: 'The poet and philosopher ______ passed away.' (Referring to one single person)
Subject–Verb Concord.explanation: When the article 'The' is used only once before the first noun ('The poet and philosopher'), both nouns refer to the same individual, taking a singular verb ('has').

Reported Speech.question: Convert to indirect speech: Rohan said to me, 'I will submit my project tomorrow.'
options: Rohan told me that he would submit his project the next day.
Rohan said to me that he will submit his project tomorrow.
Rohan told me that I would submit my project the next day.
Rohan asked me if he would submit his project the following day.
Reported Speech.correctAnswer: Rohan told me that he would submit his project the next day.
Reported Speech.conceptTag: Statements: Pronoun, Tense, and Time Adverbial Shift
Reported Speech.explanation: In past reporting of statements, 'will' shifts to 'would', 'I/my' shifts to third-person 'he/his', and 'tomorrow' shifts to 'the next day'.

Reported Speech.question: Convert to indirect speech: The teacher said to the girl, 'Have you completed your homework?'
options: The teacher asked the girl if she had completed her homework.
The teacher asked the girl that had she completed her homework.
The teacher told the girl whether she has completed her homework.
The teacher inquired the girl if had she completed her homework.
Reported Speech.correctAnswer: The teacher asked the girl if she had completed her homework.
Reported Speech.explanation: Yes/No questions use 'if' or 'whether' as the linker, drop the conjunction 'that', and invert question order ('Have you') into statement order ('she had').

Reported Speech.question: Convert to indirect speech: The stranger said to me, 'Where is the nearest post office?'
options: The stranger asked me where the nearest post office was.
The stranger asked me where was the nearest post office.
The stranger said to me that where the nearest post office was.
The stranger asked me where is the nearest post office.
Reported Speech.correctAnswer: The stranger asked me where the nearest post office was.
Reported Speech.conceptTag: Questions: Wh- Question Word Order in Indirect Speech
Reported Speech.explanation: In indirect Wh- questions, the auxiliary verb ('was') must come AFTER the subject ('the nearest post office'), never before it.

Reported Speech.question: Convert to indirect speech: Mother said to me, 'Do not waste your time on mobile games.'
options: Mother advised me not to waste my time on mobile games.
Mother forbade me not to waste my time on mobile games.
Mother told me to not wasted my time on mobile games.
Mother said to me that do not waste my time.
Reported Speech.correctAnswer: Mother advised me not to waste my time on mobile games.
Reported Speech.explanation: Negative commands/advice convert using 'advised/ordered + object + not to + base verb'.

Reported Speech.question: Convert to indirect speech: The old man said to the boy, 'Please help me cross this busy road.'
options: The old man requested the boy to help him cross that busy road.
The old man ordered the boy please to help him cross this road.
The old man requested to the boy that he should help him.
The old man asked the boy to please helped him cross that road.
Reported Speech.correctAnswer: The old man requested the boy to help him cross that busy road.
Reported Speech.explanation: The word 'Please' is replaced by the reporting verb 'requested', followed by 'object + to + V1', and 'this' shifts to 'that'.

Reported Speech.question: When does the verb tense inside the reported speech NOT change even if the statement is reported later?
options: When the reporting verb is in the Present or Future tense (e.g., 'He says' or 'He will say')
When the sentence contains a pronoun
When the speaker is asking a question
When the sentence has more than ten words
Reported Speech.correctAnswer: When the reporting verb is in the Present or Future tense (e.g., 'He says' or 'He will say')
Reported Speech.explanation: If the reporting verb is in the Present ('says') or Future ('will say'), the tense of the verb inside the quotation marks remains unchanged.

Reported Speech.question: Convert to indirect speech: Priya said, 'I bought a new dictionary yesterday.'
options: Priya said that she had bought a new dictionary the previous day.
Priya said that she bought a new dictionary yesterday.
Priya told that she has bought a new dictionary the day before.
Priya said that I had bought a new dictionary the previous day.
Reported Speech.correctAnswer: Priya said that she had bought a new dictionary the previous day.
Reported Speech.conceptTag: Statements: Simple Past to Past Perfect Shift
Reported Speech.explanation: Simple Past ('bought') backshifts to Past Perfect ('had bought'), and 'yesterday' changes to 'the previous day / the day before'.

Reported Speech.question: Convert to indirect speech: The librarian said to the students, 'Keep quiet in the reading room.'
options: The librarian instructed the students to keep quiet in the reading room.
The librarian requested the students that they keep quiet.
The librarian asked the students if they keep quiet.
The librarian said to students to kept quiet in the reading room.
Reported Speech.correctAnswer: The librarian instructed the students to keep quiet in the reading room.
Reported Speech.explanation: Imperative instructions convert the base verb into an infinitive ('to keep') after reporting verbs like 'instructed', 'ordered', or 'told'.
